title: Generic Functions
summary: Write functions with type parameters, so the type that comes out follows the type that goes in, and pass type arguments when inference has nothing to go on.
intro: Some functions don't care what they hold. The first item of an array is the first item whether the array holds numbers or users. Typing such a function with `any` throws the type away, and writing one copy per type repeats the same code. A generic function takes a type as a parameter instead, so every call gets back exactly the type it passed in. In this lesson you write your own generic functions and learn to read the generic signatures of built-ins like `map`.

steps.title: Type parameters

examples.title: First item
examples.prompt: Call one generic `first` on an array of numbers, an array of strings, and an empty array.
examples.output:
First score: 88
First name: ANA
First waiting: nobody
examples.explanation: Each call infers its own `T`. `scores` is a `number[]`, so the first call returns `number | undefined`, and `names` makes the second return `string | undefined`, as the bubbles show. Because `firstName` holds a string whenever it holds anything, `?.toUpperCase()` is allowed on it. `waiting` is empty, so `first` returns `undefined` and `??` supplies the fallback. One function serves every array, and no result loses its type.

examples.title: Wrap a value
examples.prompt: Wrap values of three different types in an object, then use each wrapped value as its own type.
examples.explanation: `T` is the type of whatever you pass, and the return type `{ value: T }` carries it along. A number in gives `{ value: number; }` back, and an object in gives back an object with every property typed. That's why `price.value.toFixed(2)` and `mug.value.sku` type-check with no annotations at the calls. In the body, `{ value }` is shorthand for `{ value: value }`.

examples.title: Why not any
examples.prompt: Write the same helper with `any` instead of a type parameter, then misspell a method on its result.
examples.errorIncludes: TypeError: firstName.toUppercase is not a function

practice.title: Last item
practice.prompt:
Make `last` generic, so it returns the last item of any array.

1. Give `last` a type parameter `T`, the parameter `xs: readonly T[]`, and the return type `T | undefined`.
2. Return the last item, or `undefined` when the array is empty.
3. Print the last temperature, the last city, and the last name in the queue, with `(none)` for an empty array.
4. Keep `export`: hidden type tests import `last` from your file.

Expected output:

```text
Last temperature: 15.3
Last city: Lima
Last in queue: (none)
```

tests.output:
Last temperature: 15.3
Last city: Lima
Last in queue: (none)

cases.name: numbers in never give strings out

hints: Start from the first example's `first`. The same signature works for `last`, and only the body changes.
`xs.at(-1)` reads the last item, and it's `undefined` when the array is empty.
The signature is `export function last<T>(xs: readonly T[]): T | undefined`.

steps.title: Several type parameters

examples.title: Pairs
examples.prompt: Pair values of different types, and let each type parameter come from its own argument.
examples.output:
Mug: 4 left
Enabled: true, groups: beta, dark-mode
examples.explanation: `A` comes from the first argument and `B` from the second. So `pair("Mug", 4)` returns a `[string, number]` tuple, and `pair(true, ["beta", "dark-mode"])` returns `[boolean, string[]]`. A tuple keeps one type per position, so destructuring gives `item` a `string` and `count` a `number`, and `flag[1]` is an array you can `join`.

examples.title: Zip two lists
examples.prompt: Combine two arrays of different types into pairs, stopping at the end of the shorter one.
examples.explanation: `A` is inferred from `names` and `B` from `scores`, so `zip` returns `[string, number][]` with no annotation at the call. Inside, `pairs` starts empty, so it's annotated with the type it will hold. With this course's `noUncheckedIndexedAccess`, `xs[i]` is `A | undefined`, so the loop checks both values before it pushes a pair. Caro has no score, so the loop stops at the shorter array's length and leaves her out.

examples.title: Passing the type yourself
examples.prompt: Create a store that starts as an empty list, then try to add an item to it.
examples.output: main.ts(12,17): error TS2345: Argument of type '"milk"' is not assignable to parameter of type 'never'.

practice.title: Chunk
practice.prompt:
Make `chunk` generic, so it splits an array of anything into groups.

1. Give `chunk` a type parameter `T`, the parameters `xs: readonly T[]` and `size: number`, and the return type `T[][]`.
2. Put the items into groups of `size`, in order. The last group holds whatever is left.
3. Print `JSON.stringify` of the seats in groups of 2, then of the guests in groups of 3.
4. Keep `export`: hidden type tests import `chunk` from your file.

Expected output:

```text
[[1,2],[3,4],[5]]
[["Ana","Ben","Caro"],["Dev","Eli"]]
```
hints: Declare `<T>` after the name, then write `T` wherever the signature says `number` for an item.
Step through the array `size` items at a time: `for (let i = 0; i < xs.length; i += size)`.
`xs.slice(i, i + size)` is one group. `slice` stops at the end of the array, so the last group can be shorter.

steps.title: Generic callbacks

examples.title: Map anything
examples.prompt: Write your own `mapArray`, then turn a list of prices into labels and into yes or no flags.
examples.explanation: Both calls pass the same `number[]`, so `T` is `number` and `cents` is a `number` in each callback. `R` differs. The first callback returns a template string, so `labels` is a `string[]`, and the second returns a comparison, so `pricey` is a `boolean[]`. The signature ties the output to the callback, which is exactly how the built-in `map` works.

examples.title: Group by a key
examples.prompt: Group orders into lists by their status, with a callback that picks each order's group.
examples.explanation: `T` is `Order`, from the array, so the callback's `o` is an `Order` and `o.status` is allowed. Each group holds the orders themselves, so the result is `Record<string, Order[]>`, as the bubble shows. `(groups[key(x)] ??= [])` creates a group the first time its key shows up, and `Object.entries` lists the groups in the order their first order appeared.

examples.title: Built-ins are generic
examples.prompt: Group the same orders with Node's built-in `Object.groupBy` and `Map.groupBy`, and read their types from the bubbles.
examples.output:
Paid: 2
Pending: 0
large: o1, o3
small: o2
examples.explanation: `Object.groupBy` is generic in both the item and the key, and its key type is whatever your callback returns. Here that's `o.status`, so the keys are `"paid" | "pending" | "shipped"`. The result is wrapped in `Partial`, which makes every key optional, because a status no order has gets no group at all. So `byStatus.pending` is `Order[] | undefined`, and here it really is missing. The Built-in Utility Types lesson covers `Partial`. `Map.groupBy` returns a `Map` instead, typed `Map<"large" | "small", Order[]>` from the two strings the callback can return.

practice.title: Count by
practice.prompt:
Make `countBy` generic, so it counts the items of any array by a key that a callback picks.

1. Give `countBy` a type parameter `T`, the parameters `xs: readonly T[]` and `key: (x: T) => string`, and the return type `Record<string, number>`.
2. For each item, call `key` and add 1 to that key's count.
3. Count `products` by their `category`, and print one `category: n` line per category, sorted by category name.
4. Keep `export`: hidden type tests import `countBy` from your file.

Expected output:

```text
garden: 1
kitchen: 3
office: 2
```

cases.name: counts numbers by a string key
the key callback must return a string

hints: The signature follows `groupBy` from the examples, with `Record<string, number>` as the result.
Count like you would by hand: `counts[k] = (counts[k] ?? 0) + 1`, where `k` is `key(x)`.
Sort the entries before the loop: `Object.entries(counts).toSorted(([a], [b]) => a.localeCompare(b))`.

recap:
- `function f<T>(...)` declares a type parameter. Each call infers `T` from its arguments, so the type of the result follows the input.
- A generic beats `any`: `any` switches checking off, while `T` keeps every result fully typed.
- Declare several type parameters with commas, like `<A, B>`. Each one is inferred from the argument where it appears.
- When inference has nothing to look at, like an empty `[]`, pass the type yourself: `createStore<string[]>([])`.
- A callback typed `(x: T) => R` lets the caller's callback decide `R`. Built-ins like `map`, `Object.groupBy`, and `Map.groupBy` are generic in exactly this way.
